newsitem.title: UK: Scottish Stone home to pipes, whisky, bomb scare.
newsitem.headline: Scottish Stone home to pipes, whisky, bomb scare.

text.p: Scotland's historic Stone of Scone, seized 700 years ago by English King Edward I, came home on Friday to a skirl of bagpipes, a dram of whisky and a bomb scare.

The Stone's crossing into Scotland at Coldstream Bridge was delayed an hour because army bomb disposal experts had to check a suspect package left on the English side. It turned out to be an empty shoe box.

Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth presided over the handover in the centre of the bridge featuring a specially composed tune played by an army piper. Both enjoyed a celebratory dram of whisky afterwards.
Coldstream is believed to be the border crossing Edward I passed through when he took the stone to England.

Since 1296, the stone has been under a throne in London's Westminster Abbey, where England's kings and queens have traditionally been crowned. It is now being taken to the Scottish capital of Edinburgh.
Once there experts will decide if it needs restoration work before it goes on view to the public at Edinburgh Castle on December 1.

It is believed the stone was first used in the coronation of a Scottish King in 839, at the village of Scone in southeast Scotland. It served as the coronation stone for all subsequent Scottish Kings until Edward I arrived to subdue Scottish rebels.

The stone disappeared in 1950 when it was stolen from Westminster Abbey and smuggled back to Scotland by a group of Scottish Nationalists, but was returned to Westminster when it was found four months later.
